Key Research Thinking Patterns: Evolutionary Bet-Hedging Modeling: Utilizing deterministic evolutionary models and Cohen's delayed germination framework to predict optimal resource allocation ratios in variable environments, specifically analyzing how predispersal herbivory by Schinia mortua drives the evolution of heterocarpy in Grindelia ciliata.

Cognitive Diagnostic Assessment: Developing and psychometrically validating rigorous diagnostic instruments, such as the Basic Evolutionary Tree-Thinking Skills Instrument (BETTSI), to identify specific cognitive barriers like left-to-right reading bias and quantify representational competence in phylogenetic reasoning.

Integrative Field-Experimental Ecology: Combining manipulative field experiments, including in situ seedbank burial and vegetative disturbance (burning/clipping), with laboratory-based viability testing (tetrazolium) and microbiome inoculation to assess recruitment bottlenecks and seedling survival in rare riparian species like Alnus maritima.

Evidence-Based Curriculum Scaffolding: Designing and evaluating pedagogical interventions, such as the Botanical Phylo-Card Game and Tree Thinking Modules, using formative/summative assessment and agnotology-based strategies to improve student data literacy and understanding of natural selection across diverse STEM audiences.
Summary Description: J. Phil Gibson is an evolutionary ecologist and STEM educator at the University of Oklahoma, bridging theoretical ecology with science education. His ecological research investigates bet-hedging strategies in Grindelia ciliata and recruitment bottlenecks in rare riparian species like Alnus maritima, employing deterministic modeling, field experiments, and microbiome analysis. Concurrently, he pioneers data literacy and phylogenetic reasoning education, developing validated diagnostic tools like the BETTSI to assess representational competence. Gibson integrates primary literature data into undergraduate curricula and mentors faculty through networks like QUBES and TIEE. His work uniquely combines rigorous empirical modeling of reproductive strategies with pedagogical innovations that enhance botanical literacy and quantitative skills, addressing both conservation challenges and cognitive barriers in science learning.
